text: A low-sugar fruit spread and a calcium-containing yoghurt drink can both use pectin, but they do not ask it to do the same job. In one, a controlled gel network is the product; in the other, the priority may be keeping protein particles dispersed while preserving a drinkable texture. Commercial citrus pectins are offered specifically for these different functions.[11]

For a low-sugar gel, the useful purchasing question is therefore not simply **“Which LM pectin replaces this one?”** It is **“Which grade sets at the right point in our process, with our acid, calcium and solids, and gives the required texture after cooling?”**

High-methoxyl pectin, or HM, has more than 50% of its carboxyl groups methyl-esterified; low-methoxyl pectin, or LM, has less than 50%. Amidated LM, often abbreviated LMA or LMAP, also contains amide groups, so its degree of amidation must be specified separately from its degree of methylation or esterification.[6][12]

The broad distinction is useful: conventional HM gelation relies on a sufficiently acidic, high-solids environment, whereas calcium-mediated LM gelation allows substantially lower-solids products.[11][12] It does not follow that all LM grades need the same calcium addition, or that all LMA grades are interchangeable.

The manufacturer's own range makes that clear. The following are selected **citrus** entries from Herbstreith & Fox's publicly hosted *The Specialists for Pectin*, pages 21–23 and 29–30; these are supplier application specifications, not results of a single comparative trial.[11]

| Named grade | DE / degree of amidation | Supplier-described function or calcium reactivity | Listed application conditions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classic CF 407 | 60–66% / — | HM, slow set | Jams and fruit preparations; TSS >58%, pH 2.9–3.3 |
| Classic CF 701 | 39–45% / — | Non-amidated LM, low calcium reactivity | Low-calorie jams, spreads and jellies; TSS 40–60%, pH 3.0–3.6 |
| Classic CF 703 | 32–38% / — | Non-amidated LM, high calcium reactivity | Low-calorie jams, spreads and jellies; TSS ≤45%, pH 3.0–3.6 |
| Amid CF 010-D | 30–36% / 14–20% | Amidated LM, medium calcium reactivity | Low-calorie jams and spreads; TSS 30–55%, pH 3.0–3.5 |
| Amid CF 020-C | 27–32% / 18–23% | Amidated LM, high calcium reactivity | Low-calorie jams and spreads; TSS 15–45%, pH 3.0–4.0 |
| Classic CM 203 | >68% / — | HM protective colloid | Low-viscosity fermented milk drinks; pH 3.6–4.2 |
| Classic CJ 206 | 68–76% / — | HM cloud stabilisation and viscosity increase | Soft drinks; pH 2.7–4.5 |

All table entries: supplier brochure.[11] TSS denotes soluble solids in the supplier's application descriptions; these ranges are not finished-product sugar analyses. The exact suffix belongs to the grade name: CF 020-C should not silently become CF 020 on a sample request.

Notice the overlap between Classic CF 703 and Amid CF 010-D. Their DE ranges overlap, but the brochure gives them different calcium-reactivity descriptions and different application windows.[11] Choosing the same DE does not select the same behaviour.

Azelis provides a second commercial example: its public listing for **GENU® Pectin LM-104 AS** describes an E440 product standardised with sucrose, with high calcium reactivity, recommended for low-sugar jams, jellies and yoghurt fruit preparations at 20–40% soluble solids.[4] That is an application description for a named supplied ingredient—not a declaration that every gram is unstandardised pectin polymer. When comparing quotations, ask how the powder is standardised and whether the proposed use level is expressed for the supplied product.

Kastner, Einhorn-Stoll and Drusch studied two commercially available citrus pectins: a non-amidated LM material with DM 30%, and an amidated LM material with DM 32% and DA 19%.[6] The nearly matched DM makes this more informative than a simple comparison between a high-DE jam grade and a low-DE gel grade.

The study used a sugar–acid model rather than a finished fruit spread. Its standard preparation contained 6 g pectin, sucrose, citric acid, sodium citrate and calcium chloride dihydrate, boiled to 900 g; total solids were maintained at 30 wt.%. The gels were prepared at least in triplicate, and the standard rheological cooling programme ran from 100°C to 10°C at 1 K/min.[6]
Three observations matter for replacement decisions.

**First, equal methylation did not give equal setting behaviour.** In the authors' direct comparison at similar calcium-to-carboxyl ratios, the amidated material developed its main structure earlier and gave a more elastic, brittle gel, while the non-amidated material was softer and more viscous in character.[6] “Amidated” is therefore not a promise of a softer spread. The desired texture still needs to be defined and measured.

**Second, lowering pH did not move both materials in the same direction.** Across the acidic conditions discussed in the paper, non-amidated LM gels became more liquid-like as pH fell, whereas the amidated material became more solid-like. The authors attributed the difference to the declining contribution of calcium bridges and the additional contribution of hydrogen bonds involving amide groups.[6] Acid adjustment after a grade change is not just a flavour correction.

**Third, calcium changes the setting process, not merely the final firmness.** Increasing calcium in the amidated system raised the initial and critical structuring temperatures; at the highest tested calcium ratio, no clear classical gel point was detectable. The authors proposed that local microgels had formed rapidly before measurement began.[6] That finding makes early thickening or local gel formation a sensible observation in a plant trial, rather than judging a replacement only by next-day firmness.

The experiment's calcium ratio was **R = 2[Ca²⁺]/[COO⁻]**, not milligrams of elemental calcium per serving.[6] It relates calcium to available dissociated carboxyl groups. Do not convert the paper into a universal calcium dose for every commercial powder: composition, ionisation and molecular structure are part of the comparison.

Herbstreith & Fox describes amidated LM pectins as forming sufficiently firm gels with relatively small calcium quantities and allowing a wider calcium concentration range.[12] Its general brochure also warns that exceeding the calcium optimum can cause a brittle gel, syneresis or formation of insoluble calcium pectinate.[11]

These statements are compatible. A wider useful window does not remove its upper boundary. Nor is the window specified by DA alone: the same supplier lists low, medium, high and very high calcium reactivity among different amidated citrus grades.[11]

The 2017 paper also illustrates why a supplier shorthand should not replace a formulation trial. Its Table 2 shows the final loss factor rising from 0.079 to 0.101 as R rises from 0.73 to 1.45; meanwhile, the reported average structure-development rate fluctuates rather than rising consistently, despite a sentence in the discussion saying that it increased.[6] We therefore do not use that sentence to claim faster overall structuring at higher calcium. The useful distinction is that **the start of setting and the texture of the cooled gel are separate responses**.

For development, test the proposed replacement alongside the incumbent across the calcium and pH range the formula will actually encounter. Keep total solids and the heating/cooling programme fixed in that first comparison. Record when structure becomes apparent, how the batch pours or fills, and the cooled product's texture and water release. This is a proposed screening design, not a reproduced recipe from the paper.

If the same powder passes at one calcium level but develops particles or loses spreadability at another, the first question should be whether the grade's reaction window fits the process—not whether to increase pectin indiscriminately.

A calcium-containing acidified milk drink is not simply a dilute low-sugar jelly. HM pectin can provide protein protection rather than a spoonable calcium-set network. The supplier brochure accordingly lists Classic CM 203 for low-viscosity fermented milk drinks, while its low-DE and amidated grades include gel and yoghurt-texture applications.[11]

An original beverage study by Liu and colleagues used an experimental CP Kelco HM pectin with DE 69%, including pectin-only drinks at 0.20% and 0.40% w/w.[13] All samples were adjusted to pH 4.0, homogenised at 180–200 bar, heated at 121°C for 4 seconds and cooled; instrumental and sensory measurements were made within one week.[13] The pectin-only samples were among the lowest-viscosity systems studied, and increasing pectin concentration reduced the measured particle sizes in the pectin-containing samples.[13]

This is evidence for an acidified protein-drink function, not a calcium-fortification trial. The pectin was experimental, and the paper does not identify its botanical source in the materials description.[13] It cannot validate a particular commercial citrus grade, extra calcium loading or months of shelf life.

There is a further purchasing trap: **HM does not mean calcium-inert.** H&F's protein-stabilisation technical guide explains that blockwise free carboxyl groups can give HM citrus pectins calcium reactivity, observable as increased viscosity after adding calcium.[12] The guide specifically advises adding pectin and calcium separately in calcium-enriched acidified drinks, and notes that lower calcium-reactive apple pectins can be advantageous in that setting.[12]

For a drink that must remain thin, this changes the sourcing brief. Request a protein-stabilising grade evaluated against the actual calcium salt, protein system and heat treatment; do not automatically choose the highest calcium-reactivity LM grade because the drink is low in sugar. A protein-free fortified juice is another task again: the casein-protection evidence above does not establish its stability.
For a low-sugar fruit spread, a useful brief could read:

> We are replacing a citrus pectin in a reduced-solids fruit spread. Please propose a non-amidated LM and, where suitable, an amidated LM candidate for our stated final pH, soluble solids and calcium system. We need sufficient flow through filling followed by the specified spreadable texture, without unacceptable particles or water release. Please provide the complete grade name, DE and DA ranges, standardisation ingredients and the application method used to characterise calcium reactivity and gel performance.

Attach the current process temperatures, residence times and cooling history, plus the fruit base and calcium salt. Ask the supplier to distinguish tests on the supplied powder from tests normalised to pectin content. The purpose is to make two samples comparable, not to accumulate certificates that do not describe setting behaviour.

For an acidified protein drink, replace that gel brief with the actual protein content, calcium addition, acidification route, homogenisation and thermal treatment, and the required drinking viscosity. H&F identifies these formulation and process variables as relevant to pectin stabilisation.[12] Evaluate sediment and particle condition alongside viscosity: a thicker drink is not automatically a better-stabilised one.[12]

The practical distinction is simple: **buy a controlled setting window for a low-sugar gel, and a validated stabilisation function for a drink.** HM, LM and DA narrow the choices; they do not finish the selection.
